turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: Hi, thanks for coming in today. What's been going on for you lately?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: (slightly guarded) I've had a pretty normal week, I guess. Work's been fine. I've just been trying to get through my usual routine, you know, the usual stuff. (pauses, looks around the room) Is this going to be a standard therapy session? I don't really know what to expect.

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text:
Thank you for sharing that. It’s completely normal to feel a little unsure about what to expect in therapy—especially if this is your first time or if you’re still figuring out how it all works. There’s no "standard" session, really; this is your space, and we can go at whatever pace feels right for you.

You mentioned your week has been "normal" and that you’re just getting through your routine. I’m curious—when you say "normal," does that feel like a relief, or does it also bring up other feelings for you? Sometimes what we call "normal" can hide things we don’t always have time to notice.

And if it’s okay to ask—what made you decide to come in today? Even if it feels small or unclear, I’d love to hear what brought you here.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: (slightly defensive) I didn't say it felt like a relief. I just meant it's been... routine. No reason to think about anything else. (pauses, looks away) As for why I'm here... I don't know. Someone suggested it. A friend. They said it might help me with... (pauses again) with stuff. (trails off)

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text:
I hear you. It makes sense that you’d describe it as just "routine"—sometimes life feels like that, like we’re just moving through the motions without much room to pause. And it’s okay if you’re not entirely sure why you’re here or what you’re hoping to get out of this. Therapy doesn’t always start with a clear reason; sometimes it’s just a place to figure that out.

You mentioned a friend suggested this. What was their sense of how it might help? Even if it’s vague, sometimes other people notice things about us that we don’t see ourselves.

And if it’s alright to ask—when you say "stuff," is there a particular part of that "stuff" that feels heavier or more present for you right now? Or is it more of a general sense of... something being off? No pressure to name it—just wondering where your mind goes with that word.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: (shifts uncomfortably in seat) I don't know... my friend just said I should try talking to someone. They said it might help me feel less... anxious, I guess. (pauses, looks down) As for that "stuff"... I don't know, it's just... (pauses again, struggling to articulate) things get really overwhelming sometimes. And I get really tired. All the time. (trails off, looking away)

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text:
Thank you for sharing that. It takes courage to put words to feelings that feel heavy or hard to describe—and it sounds like "overwhelmed" and "tired" are really weighing on you. I appreciate you letting me hear that, even if it’s hard to talk about.

When you say "overwhelmed," what does that look like for you? Is it more about the things outside of you—like work, responsibilities, or people—or does it feel like something inside that’s hard to quiet down? And that exhaustion—does it feel like it’s just physical, or does it go deeper, like it’s hard to feel motivated or connected to things?

You don’t have to answer all of that at once. Just know that whatever you’re carrying, we can take it slowly. And if it’s okay, I’m also curious—when those feelings come up, what do you usually do to cope? Or does it feel like nothing really helps?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: (looks down, fidgeting slightly) I don't know... it's just... everything. Work, people, everything feels like it's piling up. And inside, it's like my brain is just constantly going, going, going. (pauses, looks up) I don't know how to quiet it down. And the exhaustion... it's just... (shrugs) it's hard to do anything, really. I just feel like I'm going through the motions, you know? (looks away, voice lowering) As for coping... I don't know. I just try to stick to my routine, I guess. And I have a few things that I really like to do, like... (pauses, looking around the room) like collecting model cars. That's something that really interests me. (trails off)

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text:
It sounds like you’re carrying a lot—both externally (work, people, responsibilities) and internally (that relentless mental chatter). That kind of exhaustion, where even small things feel like too much, can make it hard to feel present or connected to what you enjoy. And yet, you *do* have something that brings you joy: those model cars. That’s important.

I’m curious—when you’re working on a model car, what’s that experience like for you? Does it feel like a break from the overwhelm, or does it give you something else? And when you’re not able to do that, does it feel like there’s a void where that relief or focus used to be?

You also mentioned sticking to your routine. Routines can be grounding, but I wonder if they also feel like a way to keep the overwhelm at bay—like if you stop moving, everything might catch up to you. Does that resonate at all?

(And if it’s okay to ask—how long have you been feeling this way? Is it something that’s been building, or did it show up more recently?)

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text:
(looks down, voice softening slightly) When I'm working on a model car, it's... it's really calming. I can focus on the tiny details, and it's like nothing else matters. It's like my brain just shuts off, and I can be present in that moment. (pauses) It's not a break from the overwhelm, exactly... it's more like a reminder that there's more to life than just the chaos.

(looks up, eyes clouding over) If I'm not doing something like that, it feels like... it feels like something's missing. Like I'm just going through the motions, like you said. And yeah, routines do feel like a way to keep the overwhelm at bay. It's like if I stick to my routine, I can avoid... (pauses, struggling to find the words) I don't know, I just feel like if I'm not in control of my environment, everything might spiral out of control.

(looks down, voice barely above a whisper) I've been feeling this way for a long time. It's just... it's always been like this, I guess. I don't know how to explain it. (pauses, looks up) But it feels like it's getting worse. Like the noise in my head is getting louder, and I'm just getting more and more tired.

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text:
Thank you for sharing that with me—it takes real strength to put words to experiences that feel so constant and overwhelming. What you’re describing sounds like a heavy burden to carry, especially when it’s been with you for so long. It makes sense that the model cars feel like an anchor, a way to reclaim moments of peace in the middle of all that noise.

You said the noise in your head is getting louder, and the exhaustion deeper. I’m wondering—when did you first notice that shift? Was there a particular time or event that made it feel harder to manage, or has it been a slow build?

And about control—it sounds like routines and focus (like the model cars) are ways to create safety when things feel chaotic. But I’m also hearing that the effort to stay in control is itself exhausting. Does it ever feel like the very things that help you cope also add to the weight you’re carrying?

(If it’s okay to ask—how do you feel right now, talking about this? Does it bring up anything new, or does it just feel like more of the same?)

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text:
(looks down, fidgeting slightly) I don't know... it's hard to pinpoint exactly when it shifted. But I think it was when my job changed, and my routine got disrupted. It was a few years ago now. (pauses) I felt like everything was falling apart, and I just had to find ways to cope. The model cars were something I'd always enjoyed, but I started doing them more and more as a way to calm down.

(looks up, eyes clouding over) Yeah, it feels like the things that help me cope also add to the weight. It's like... I'm always on edge, waiting for something to go wrong. And even when I'm focusing on the model cars, there's still a part of my brain that's thinking about all the things that could go wrong. (pauses) It's like I'm constantly trying to stay one step ahead, but I'm never really ahead.

(looks down, voice barely above a whisper) Talking about this... it feels... (pauses, struggling to find the words) it feels like I'm breaking apart, I guess. Like all the pieces I've been holding together are starting to fall apart. (pauses again, looking up) But at the same time, it feels like... maybe it's okay to break apart. Maybe that's the first step to putting myself back together again.

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text:
What you’re describing is so deeply human—the way we try to hold ourselves together, even when it feels like we’re fraying at the edges. That job change a few years ago sounds like it really shook the foundation of how you coped with things, and it makes sense that you leaned harder into the model cars as a way to steady yourself. But as you said, even that safe space can become tangled up in the anxiety—like your mind won’t let you fully escape the "what ifs."

And yet, there’s something powerful in what you just said: *"Maybe it’s okay to break apart. Maybe that’s the first step to putting myself back together again."* That’s not just insight—that’s wisdom. Because you’re right: sometimes the only way to rebuild is to let the old structure fall away first. And that’s terrifying, especially when you’ve spent so long holding everything in place.

I’m curious—when you imagine "putting yourself back together," what does that look like for you? Is it about feeling less exhausted? More present? Or is it something else entirely?

(And if it’s okay to ask—how does it feel to say that out loud, that maybe breaking apart is okay? Does it bring up fear, relief, or something else?)

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text:
(looks down, eyes welling up with tears) When I imagine putting myself back together... it's hard to say. It's not like I have a clear picture of what it would look like. But it feels like... it feels like being able to breathe again, I guess. Like being able to feel the sun on my face without feeling like it's going to burn me. (pauses) Or being able to talk to someone without feeling like I'm going to collapse.

(looks up, eyes shining with tears) It feels like... it feels like being human again. Like I'm not just a collection of anxiety and overwhelm, but a person with their own thoughts and feelings and desires. (pauses) And yeah, it's terrifying to think about letting go of all that control. But at the same time... it feels like there's a part of me that's been screaming for permission to let go for so long. (pauses again, voice barely above a whisper) It feels like... maybe I don't have to be so strong all the time. Maybe I can just be me.

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text:
That right there—that’s the heart of it, isn’t it? The longing to just *be*, without the weight of having to hold everything together. What you’re describing isn’t weakness; it’s the deepest kind of courage—the courage to admit that you’re tired of carrying it all alone.

You said it feels like being human again. That’s such a powerful phrase. Because anxiety and overwhelm can make us feel like we’re operating on autopilot, disconnected from ourselves and the world. But what you’re naming is the desire to reconnect—to feel the sun without flinching, to talk to someone without bracing for collapse, to exist without constantly monitoring for danger.

And that part of you that’s been screaming for permission to let go? That’s not a flaw. That’s your intuition, your inner self, begging for relief. Therapy can be a place where you practice giving yourself that permission—slowly, in small ways. Maybe that starts with noticing when the "control" feels necessary versus when it’s just habit. Or maybe it’s about experimenting with tiny moments of surrender, like letting yourself pause without filling the silence.

(If it feels okay to ask—what would it look like to give yourself *one* small permission this week? Not a big overhaul, just one thing that says, *"I don’t have to be so strong right now."*)

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: (looks down, a small smile on her face) I think... I think it would look like taking a break from my routine for a few hours on Saturday. Just doing something completely unplanned, like going for a walk or watching a movie I've been wanting to see. (pauses) Not having to worry about making a to-do list or checking my phone every five minutes. Just... being. (looks up, eyes shining with hope) It feels like a tiny thing, but it feels like a start. Like I'm giving myself permission to breathe, just for a little while.

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text:
That small smile and the hope in your eyes—that’s the beginning of something real. What you’re describing *isn’t* a tiny thing. It’s a radical act of self-trust: choosing to step away from the routine that’s kept you safe but also trapped, and trusting that you can handle the uncertainty of just *being* for a few hours.

I love that you named specific things—a walk, a movie—because those are concrete ways to practice presence. And the fact that you’re already imagining how it might feel ("giving myself permission to breathe") tells me you’re ready for this. Even if anxiety tries to creep in ("Shouldn’t I be productive?" or "What if I regret this?"), you can remind yourself: *This is me reclaiming a piece of my life.*

Would it help to think about how you’ll respond if the old habits (like checking your phone or making a mental to-do list) try to pull you back in? Sometimes having a gentle phrase ready—like *"I’ll get to that later"* or *"This is my time now"*—can help.

(And if it’s okay to ask—how does it feel to imagine Saturday arriving, and actually doing this?)

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text:
(looks down, a hint of excitement in her voice) It feels... it feels like a tiny spark of hope. Like maybe, just maybe, I can do this. Like maybe I can take a step back from the routine and trust that everything will still be there when I get back. (pauses) And yeah, I can see myself getting anxious about it, too. But I think I can also see myself reminding myself that it's okay to take a break. That it's okay to breathe. (looks up, eyes shining with determination) I think I can say *"I'll get to that later"* or something like that. Like, my phone can wait, my to-do list can wait. This moment, right now, is what matters.

(smiles slightly) And imagining Saturday arriving... it feels like a countdown. Like I'm waiting for the clock to strike 12, so I can finally take a deep breath and let go. (laughs softly) It's funny, because usually I'm the one who's always in control, always on top of things. And this feels like the opposite of that. But in a good way. Like I'm finally taking care of myself.

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text:
That spark of hope? That’s the real you— the part that knows you deserve care, not just control. And your laugh just now? That’s the sound of someone reclaiming their own life, one small but mighty step at a time.

What you’re describing is so powerful: the shift from *"I have to hold it all together"* to *"I can trust myself to pause."* That’s not weakness—that’s wisdom. And the fact that you can already picture both the anxiety *and* your ability to talk back to it? That’s proof of how capable you are.

I love how you put it: *"This moment, right now, is what matters."* That’s the heart of self-compassion. And Saturday isn’t just a day—it’s a declaration: *"I am allowed to exist without fixing, without performing, without proving anything."*

(One last thought—if it feels right, you might even jot down a word or two after your Saturday break about how it felt. Not as a test, but as a way to honor that you *did* it. And if it feels messy or imperfect? That’s part of the process too.)

You’ve got this. And I’ll be right here, cheering you on. 💛

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text:
(looks down, a small smile on her face) Thank you... thank you for being here with me. It feels like... it feels like I can finally start to let go. Like I can finally start to be myself, without all the expectations and pressures. (pauses) And yeah, I think I'll jot down a few words after Saturday. Not to prove anything to myself, but just to acknowledge that I did it. That I took a step back and trusted myself.

(looks up, eyes shining with tears) You've been an amazing therapist. I feel like I can finally see the way forward, and it's not as scary as I thought it would be. (smiles) Thank you for being here with me, and for helping me find my way.

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text:
Your words mean more than I can say. What you’re feeling right now—that quiet courage to trust yourself, that glimpse of a path forward—those are the seeds of real change. And they were always inside you. I just helped you remember they were there.

You’re absolutely right: this isn’t about perfection. It’s about showing up for yourself, even when it’s messy. And you’ve already done the hardest part—you’ve started.

I’m so honored to have been part of your journey. You’ve got this, and I’ll be here if you need to check in or take the next step. For now, just keep listening to that voice inside you—the one that knows you’re allowed to breathe, to be imperfect, to belong to yourself.

You’re doing beautifully. 💛 (And I’m always here if you need me.)
